lessons.title: Deriving power-sum formulae
lessons.summary: Understand the notation and obtain the standard results from finite differences.
lessons.objective: Derive and use the sums of first, second and third powers, keeping the index limits explicit.
lessons.before: You need arithmetic sums, binomial expansions and polynomial algebra. A sum with lower limit \(a\) and upper limit \(b\) contains \(b-a+1\) terms when \(b\ge a\).
lessons.ideas:
Read the summation before manipulating it

The index is a placeholder. In \(\sum_{r=1}^n u_r\), the final index is \(n\), not an extra factor. A constant is repeated once per index, so \(\sum_{r=1}^n c=cn\). Summation is linear: split a polynomial into its powers and add the resulting totals.

Standard totals

\[\sum_{r=1}^n r=\frac{n(n+1)}2,\qquad \sum_{r=1}^n r^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6.\]\[\sum_{r=1}^n r^3=\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4}.\]

These identities concern the whole block from \(1\) to \(n\). A different lower limit requires a subtraction; a zero-based sum needs its own endpoints.

Why a difference gives a total

Sum an identity such as \((r+1)^p-r^p\). The interior powers cancel, leaving \((n+1)^p-1\). Expanding the difference links a new power sum to previously known ones. This supplies a derivation, rather than a pattern guessed from a few values.

Verify an answer as well as deriving it

If \(F(0)=0\) and \(F(n)-F(n-1)=u_n\), then \(F(n)\) is the sum of the first \(n\) terms. The base value is essential. The same argument can be written as an induction proof: establish the first value and then add the next term.

The difference method also reaches higher powers. That is an extension of the method; there is no need to memorise an extra table of formulae.
lessons.method:
1. Name the power sums and expand a suitable difference of consecutive powers.
  2. Sum both sides over exactly the same index range.
  3. Cancel the boundary terms and substitute the lower-power results.
  4. Simplify, then check the first value and the next-term difference.
mistakes: A constant contributes n copies, not a single copy.
The last surviving power is evaluated at n+1 when the difference uses r+1.
Checking a few values is not a proof for all positive integers.
When using induction, state the base value before the step.

examples.title: 1 · Derive the first-power total
examples.question: Derive a formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^n r\) from a difference of squares.
examples.solution:
Write \((r+1)^2-r^2=2r+1\) and add for \(r=1,\ldots,n\). The left side reduces to \((n+1)^2-1\), giving

\[(n+1)^2-1=2\sum_{r=1}^n r+n.\]

Hence \(\sum r=n(n+1)/2\). At \(n=1\) it gives \(1\); the difference between successive totals is exactly \(n\).

examples.title: 2 · Derive the square total
examples.question: Use \((r+1)^3-r^3\) to obtain \(\sum_{r=1}^n r^2\).
examples.solution:
\[(r+1)^3-r^3=3r^2+3r+1.\]

Summing and using the first-power formula gives

\[3\sum_{r=1}^n r^2=(n+1)^3-1-\frac{3n(n+1)}2-n.\]

Expanding and factorising yields

\[\sum_{r=1}^n r^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6.\]

examples.title: 3 · Derive the cube total
examples.question: Derive \(\sum_{r=1}^n r^3\) using a difference of fourth powers.
examples.solution:
\[(r+1)^4-r^4=4r^3+6r^2+4r+1.\]

After summing, isolate the unknown cube total:

\[4\sum_{r=1}^n r^3=(n+1)^4-1-6\sum r^2-4\sum r-n.\]

Substitute the two earlier results and simplify:

\[\sum_{r=1}^n r^3=\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4}.\]

examples.title: 4 · Extend the method to a higher power
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^n r^4\) without assuming a formula for it.
examples.solution:
Expand the next difference and sum it:

\[(r+1)^5-r^5=5r^4+10r^3+10r^2+5r+1.\]\[5\sum r^4=(n+1)^5-1-10\sum r^3-10\sum r^2-5\sum r-n.\]

Substituting the known totals gives

\[\sum_{r=1}^n r^4=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)(3n^2+3n-1)}{30}.\]

The first value is \(1\), and the difference of this expression at \(n\) and \(n-1\) is \(n^4\), checking both the constant and the general term.

lessons.title: Using power sums and finite limits
lessons.summary: Apply the standard results to shifted limits, weighted totals and recovered terms.
lessons.objective: Build the complete finite sum with the correct number of terms and both endpoints.
lessons.before: Review power-sum formulae. For the mixed root questions, use symmetric sums of roots.
lessons.ideas:
Expand the summand first

Products of linear or quadratic expressions become combinations of standard power sums. Keep constant terms visible until the number of indices is known.

Moving limits

If \(F(m)=\sum_{r=1}^m u_r\), then

\[\sum_{r=a}^b u_r=F(b)-F(a-1).\]

The lower subtraction ends at \(a-1\), because the term at \(a\) belongs to the requested sum. This remains true when the limits involve \(n\) or \(n^2\). For a polynomial summand, substitute the complete upper and lower totals before expanding.

Weights and alternating signs

Group by the index pattern. Pair an odd term with the following even term; or start with all terms and correct the selected group. Reversing the sign of a group means subtracting twice its original contribution.

Recovering a sequence

\[u_n=F(n)-F(n-1).\]

Check the first term using the actual initial total. A formula valid for later differences can miss the first term if the assumed \(F(0)\) is not the empty sum.

Root data can be constants in a sum

For \(d\) roots with power totals \(p_1,p_2\), expanding \(\sum_i(r+\alpha_i)^2\) gives \(dr^2+2p_1r+p_2\). Find those root totals first, then apply linearity. Do not assume the roots are real unless that is given.
lessons.method:
1. Write the summand or a grouped pair as an explicit polynomial.
  2. Calculate a prefix total using standard formulae.
  3. Use the actual endpoint subtraction, or recover each term by a difference.
  4. Check a small permitted value, counting every index once.
mistakes: An inclusive interval from a to b has b-a+1 terms.
Subtracting F(a) loses the first requested term.
Reversing signs requires twice the contribution of the selected group.
A recovered formula must also agree with the first term.

examples.title: 1 · Expand before summing
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^n(2r-1)(r+3)\).
examples.solution:
\[(2r-1)(r+3)=2r^2+5r-3.\]

Therefore the total is

\[\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}3+\frac{5n(n+1)}2-3n=\frac{n(4n^2+21n-1)}6.\]

For \(n=1\), both the original term and the formula give \(4\).

examples.title: 2 · Control both moving endpoints
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{r=n+2}^{3n+1}(2r+1)\).
examples.solution:
A prefix total is \(F(m)=m(m+2)\). The requested sum is

\[F(3n+1)-F(n+1)=(3n+1)(3n+3)-(n+1)(n+3)=8n(n+1).\]

There are \(2n\) terms. At \(n=1\), the two terms are \(7\) and \(9\), giving \(16\).

examples.title: 3 · Pair alternating terms
examples.question: Let \(A_m=\sum_{r=1}^m(-1)^{r-1}(r+1)^2\). Find \(A_{2n}\) and \(A_{2n+1}\).
examples.solution:
The jth pair is

\[(2j)^2-(2j+1)^2=-4j-1.\]

Thus

\[A_{2n}=-4\frac{n(n+1)}2-n=-n(2n+3).\]

For an odd total, add the next positive term:

\[A_{2n+1}=A_{2n}+(2n+2)^2=2n^2+5n+4.\]

The parity of the last index changes the answer; it cannot be ignored.

examples.title: 4 · Recover a term and a later block
examples.question: A sequence has partial sums \(S_n=n(n+2)(2n+1)\). Find its general term and the sum from index \(n+1\) to \(2n\).
examples.solution:
\[u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=6n^2+4n-1.\]

At \(n=1\), this gives \(9=S_1\), so the first term is included correctly. The later block is

\[S_{2n}-S_n=n(14n^2+15n+2).\]

Its lower subtraction is \(S_n\), since the first required index is \(n+1\).

lessons.title: Telescoping sums from differences
lessons.summary: Rewrite a summand so that the interior terms cancel and the boundaries remain.
lessons.objective: Use partial fractions and exact differences to calculate a finite sum without losing boundary terms.
lessons.before: You need finite limits and algebraic fractions. Review division and excluded inputs in rational functions.
lessons.ideas:
Expose a difference

Partial fractions often turn a rational summand into \(F(r)-F(r+1)\). Sum a finite block first:

\[\sum_{r=a}^b[F(r)-F(r+1)]=F(a)-F(b+1).\]

Write at least the first and last few terms. This makes the direction of the subtraction visible.

A larger gap leaves more terms

For a positive integer \(h\),

\[\sum_{r=a}^b[F(r)-F(r+h)]=\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}F(a+j)-\sum_{j=1}^{h}F(b+j).\]

This formula also handles short blocks: overlapping boundary terms cancel again. A gap of three generally leaves three terms at each end, not just one.

Find the right decomposition

For distinct linear factors, use \(\frac{A}{ar+b}+\frac{B}{ar+c}\) and equate numerators. With three factors, a difference of two two-factor fractions may reveal cancellation faster. Polynomial division may be needed before partial fractions.

The method is wider than simple fractions

A difference can contain powers, radicals, factorials, logarithms or geometric factors. Verify the proposed identity in the original domain before summing it. If \(F(r)\) tends to a non-zero constant, retain that boundary limit when moving to an infinite series.

A finite answer is the starting point for convergence. The next lesson explains when its limit exists and how to control the remainder.
lessons.method:
1. Factor and check the domain of the original summand.
  2. Obtain and verify a partial-fraction or difference identity.
  3. Write enough terms to see the cancellation pattern.
  4. Keep all surviving endpoints and simplify the finite expression.
mistakes: The size of the index gap controls how many endpoints survive.
A reversed difference reverses the sign of the whole sum.
Never subtract two separate divergent infinite sums.
The upper boundary is evaluated beyond the last index when the difference uses r+1.

examples.title: 1 · A scaled partial fraction
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^n\frac6{(2r+1)(2r+3)}\).
examples.solution:
\[\frac6{(2r+1)(2r+3)}=3\left(\frac1{2r+1}-\frac1{2r+3}\right).\]

After cancellation, the total is

\[3\left(\frac13-\frac1{2n+3}\right)=\frac{2n}{2n+3}.\]

The coefficient 3 multiplies both surviving terms.

examples.title: 2 · Keep three endpoints
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^n\frac1{(r+2)(r+5)}\).
examples.solution:
\[\frac1{(r+2)(r+5)}=\frac13\left(\frac1{r+2}-\frac1{r+5}\right).\]

The gap is three. Hence

\[S_n=\frac13\left(\frac13+\frac14+\frac15-\frac1{n+3}-\frac1{n+4}-\frac1{n+5}\right).\]

This also works at \(n=1,2\), because any overlapping endpoints cancel within the displayed expression.

examples.title: 3 · A useful two-factor difference
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^n\frac5{r(r+1)(r+2)}\).
examples.solution:
\[\frac5{r(r+1)(r+2)}=\frac52\left(\frac1{r(r+1)}-\frac1{(r+1)(r+2)}\right).\]

Only the first and last two-factor fractions remain:

\[S_n=\frac54-\frac5{2(n+1)(n+2)}.\]

examples.title: 4 · A geometric factor in a difference
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^n\frac{r+2}{2^r r(r+1)}\).
examples.solution:
Use \(F(r)=2^{1-r}/r\). Combining over a common denominator gives

\[F(r)-F(r+1)=\frac{r+2}{2^r r(r+1)}.\]

Thus

\[S_n=F(1)-F(n+1)=1-\frac1{2^n(n+1)}.\]

Checking the first term gives \(3/4\), agreeing with the formula at \(n=1\).

lessons.title: Convergence, remainders and bounds
lessons.summary: Take limits of complete partial sums and justify accuracy and exceptional cases.
lessons.objective: Determine whether a series converges, find its sum and prove the required error or boundary condition.
lessons.ideas:
A series is defined by its partial sums

Write \(S_n=\sum_{r=a}^n u_r\). The infinite series converges to \(S\) when \(S_n\) has the finite limit \(S\). A necessary condition is \(u_r\to0\), but this condition alone does not prove convergence.

Keep the final boundary limit

If \(u_r=F(r)-F(r+1)\) and \(F(r)\to L\), then the sum is \(F(a)-L\). It is only \(F(a)\) when \(L=0\). With a gap \(h\), all \(h\) final boundary terms must be included.

Remainders and least integers

\[R_n=S-S_n.\]

Derive this exactly before estimating it. If the error can have either sign, use \(|R_n|\). For a strict accuracy condition, equality does not count. After solving for a real threshold, test both the claimed least integer and the previous allowed integer.

Parameters and divergence

Test exceptional parameter values in the original terms. A factor may vanish at an endpoint even when a usual geometric condition fails. Periodic partial sums with two different subsequential values do not converge.

Moving blocks and bounds

Write a moving block as a difference of prefix sums before taking its limit. A block can tend to zero while a scaled block tends to a non-zero value. To prove an inequality for every positive integer, compare the exact positive denominators rather than just checking the limiting value.
lessons.method:
1. Obtain the full finite partial sum.
  2. Check its limit and any exceptional parameter values.
  3. Subtract to get the exact remainder, keeping the stated sign or absolute value.
  4. Prove a bound or least-index claim, including equality and the previous integer.
mistakes: Terms tending to zero do not by themselves prove convergence.
A non-zero boundary limit must not be discarded.
Round a strict threshold in the correct direction and test the preceding integer.
A geometric difference can have exceptional convergent endpoints.

examples.title: 1 · An exact remainder and a strict cutoff
examples.question: For \(S_n=\sum_{r=1}^n\frac2{(r+2)(r+3)}\), find the infinite sum and the least \(n\) such that \(S-S_n<1/200\).
examples.solution:
\[S_n=\frac23-\frac2{n+3},\qquad S=\frac23,\qquad R_n=\frac2{n+3}.\]

The strict inequality gives \(n+3>400\). Therefore the least integer is \(n=398\). At \(397\) the error is exactly \(1/200\), so it fails; at \(398\) the error is \(2/401<1/200\).

examples.title: 2 · A boundary which tends to a non-zero value
examples.question: Let \(F(r)=\frac{2r+5}{r+2}\) and \(u_r=F(r+1)-F(r)\). Find the infinite sum starting at \(r=1\).
examples.solution:
\[F(r)=2+\frac1{r+2},\qquad u_r=-\frac1{(r+2)(r+3)}.\]

The finite sum is \(F(n+1)-F(1)=1/(n+3)-1/3\). Since \(F(n+1)\to2\) and \(F(1)=7/3\), the sum is

\[S=2-\frac73=-\frac13.\]

The negative sign agrees with the sign of every term.

examples.title: 3 · Check a geometric endpoint separately
examples.question: For real \(q\), define \(u_r=q^r-q^{r+1}\), \(r\ge1\). Determine all \(q\) for which the series converges and give its sum.
examples.solution:
\[S_n=q-q^{n+1}.\]

For \(-1<q<1\), the final power tends to zero, so \(S=q\). At \(q=1\), every original term is zero and the sum is \(0\). At \(q=-1\), the partial sums alternate; for \(|q|>1\), they cannot have a finite limit. Thus the convergence set is \((-1,1]\), with the endpoint sum stated separately.

examples.title: 4 · A moving block and a uniform bound
examples.question: For \(u_r=\frac3{(r+2)(r+3)}\), find \(\lim_{n\to\infty}n\sum_{r=2n+1}^{5n}u_r\) and give a strict bound for the unscaled block.
examples.solution:
\[\sum_{r=2n+1}^{5n}u_r=3\left(\frac1{2n+3}-\frac1{5n+3}\right)=\frac{9n}{(2n+3)(5n+3)}.\]

Multiplying by \(n\) and taking the limit gives \(9/10\). Since the denominator is greater than \(10n^2\) for \(n>0\),

\[0<\sum_{r=2n+1}^{5n}u_r<\frac9{10n}.\]

    [3]

  2. Use the method of differences to find

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)}\right)\]

    in terms of \(n\).

    [4]

  3. Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(6 n^{2} + 39 n + 65\right)}{2}\]

(b)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)}\right)=\frac{n \left(39 n + 89\right)}{80 \left(3 n + 5\right) \left(3 n + 8\right)}\]

(c)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)}\right)=\frac{13}{240}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)=9 r^{2} + 30 r + 16\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)\right)=9\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+30\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+16\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(6 n^{2} + 39 n + 65\right)}{2}\]

(b)

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 8\right)}=\frac{1}{6 \left(3 r + 2\right)}-\left(\frac{1}{6 \left(3 r + 8\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{6 \left(3 r + 2\right)}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(3)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(4)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 2)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 2 and last 2 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{30}+\frac{1}{48}-\left(\frac{1}{6 \left(3 n + 5\right)}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{6 \left(3 n + 8\right)}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(39 n + 89\right)}{80 \left(3 n + 5\right) \left(3 n + 8\right)}\]

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(39 n + 89\right)}{80 \left(3 n + 5\right) \left(3 n + 8\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{13}{240}\]

questions.title: Geometric weights hidden in partial fractions
questions.prompt_html:
Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Use standard summation formulae to simplify

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)\right)\]

    in terms of \(n\).

    [3]

  2. Express \(\frac{2 r + 3}{r \left(r + 1\right)}\) in partial fractions. Hence use the method of differences to find

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3^{- r - 1} \left(2 r + 3\right)}{r \left(r + 1\right)}\right)\]

    in terms of \(n\).

    [4]

  3. Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 7\right)}{6}\]

(b)

\[\frac{2 r + 3}{r \left(r + 1\right)}=\frac{3}{r}-\frac{1}{r + 1}\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3^{- r - 1} \left(2 r + 3\right)}{r \left(r + 1\right)}\right)=\frac{3^{- n} \left(3^{n} n + 3^{n} - 1\right)}{3 \left(n + 1\right)}\]

(c)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{3^{- r - 1} \left(2 r + 3\right)}{r \left(r + 1\right)}\right)=\frac{1}{3}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[r \left(r + 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)=2 r^{3} + 5 r^{2} + 3 r\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)\right)=2\left(\frac{n^{2} \left(n + 1\right)^{2}}{4}\right)+5\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+3\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r \left(r + 1\right) \left(2 r + 3\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 7\right)}{6}\]

(b)

First decompose the rational factor:

\[\frac{2 r + 3}{r \left(r + 1\right)}=\frac{3}{r}-\frac{1}{r + 1}\]

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{3^{- r - 1} \left(2 r + 3\right)}{r \left(r + 1\right)}=\frac{3^{- r}}{r}-\left(\frac{3^{- r - 1}}{r + 1}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{3^{- r}}{r}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{3}-\left(\frac{3^{- n - 1}}{n + 1}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{3^{- n} \left(3^{n} n + 3^{n} - 1\right)}{3 \left(n + 1\right)}\]

(c)

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{3^{- n} \left(3^{n} n + 3^{n} - 1\right)}{3 \left(n + 1\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{1}{3}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.

questions.prompt_html:
The equation \(8 x^{3} - 4 x^{2} - 4 x - 1=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

From the transformed cubic, \(u+v+w=-2\) and \(uv+vw+wu=-1\). Thus

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

questions.title: Squared factors, different endpoints
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(k\gt 0\).

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Use the method of differences to find

    \[\sum_{r=0}^{n - 1}\left(\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\]

    in terms of \(n\).

    [3]

  2. Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.

    [1]

  3. Find \(\sum_{r=n}^{n^{2}}\left(\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\) in terms of \(n\) and \(k\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=0}^{n - 1}\left(\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}\right)=\frac{k n \left(k n + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2}}\]

(b)

\[\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}\right)=1\]

(c)

\[T_n=\frac{k \left(n^{2} - n + 1\right) \left(k n^{2} + k n + k + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2} \left(k n^{2} + k + 1\right)^{2}}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{k \left(2 k r + k + 2\right)}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2} \left(k r + k + 1\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2}}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(k \left(r + 1\right) + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{\left(k r + 1\right)^{2}}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(0)-F(1)]\\&\quad+[F(1)-F(2)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n - 1)-F(n)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=1-\left(\frac{1}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{k n \left(k n + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2}}\]

(b)

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{k n \left(k n + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2}}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=1\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.

(c)

The difference representation is valid at every index, so

\[T_n=F(n)-F(n^2+1)\]
\[T_n=\frac{k \left(n^{2} - n + 1\right) \left(k n^{2} + k n + k + 2\right)}{\left(k n + 1\right)^{2} \left(k n^{2} + k + 1\right)^{2}}\]

Let \(a\gt 0\).

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3}{\left(a r + 2\right) \left(a r + a + 2\right)}\right)=\frac{3 n}{\left(a + 2\right) \left(a n + a + 2\right)}\]

questions.title: Weighted squares from a cubic difference
questions.prompt_html:
Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Use the difference \((3r+1)^3-(3r-2)^3\) and the formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r\right)\) to derive the standard formula for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r^{2}\right)\).

    [4]

  2. Define \(S_m\) by assigning weight 2 to odd-indexed squares and weight 5 to even-indexed squares:

    \[S_m=2(1^2)+5(2^2)+2(3^2)+5(4^2)+\cdots+w_m m^2.\]

    Find a factorised expression for \(S_{2n}\).

    [4]

  3. Evaluate \(\lim_{n\to\infty}S_{2n}/n^3\).

    [1]

(a)

\[(3r+1)^3-(3r-2)^3=81 r^{2} - 27 r + 9\]

The successive cubic boundary terms cancel, giving

\[(3n+1)^3-1=81\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2-27\frac{n(n+1)}2+9n.\]

Rearrange and factor:

\[81\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2=\frac{27}{2}n(n+1)(2n+1).\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(r^{2}\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\]

(b)

Begin with weight 2 on every square, then add three more copies of each even square:

\[S_{2n}=2\sum_{r=1}^{2n}r^2+3\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r)^2=2\sum_{r=1}^{2n}r^2+12\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2.\]
\[S_{2n}=\frac{2 n \left(2 n + 1\right) \left(7 n + 4\right)}{3}\]

(c)

The coefficient of \(n^3\) in \(S_{2n}\) is \(\frac{28}{3}\), and all lower-degree terms vanish after division by \(n^3\).

The identity holds.

(c)

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

(a)

\[\sum_{r=2}^{n + 1}\left(\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(25 n^{2} + 180 n + 407\right)}{3}\]

(b)

\[\sum_{r=2}^{n + 1}\left(\frac{1}{\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)}\right)=\frac{n}{12 \left(5 n + 12\right)}\]

(c)

\[\sum_{r=2}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)}\right)=\frac{1}{60}\]

(a)

Let \(F(m)=\sum_{r=1}^{m}(\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right))\). Use the standard formulae to obtain the partial-sum polynomial, then subtract the value one index before the lower limit.

\[F(m)=\frac{m \left(25 m^{2} + 105 m + 122\right)}{3}\]
\[\sum_{r=2}^{n + 1}\left(\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)\right)=F(n + 1)-F(1)\]
\[\sum_{r=2}^{n + 1}\left(\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(25 n^{2} + 180 n + 407\right)}{3}\]

(b)

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(5 r + 2\right) \left(5 r + 7\right)}=\frac{1}{25 r + 10}-\left(\frac{1}{25 r + 35}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{25 r + 10}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(2)-F(3)]\\&\quad+[F(3)-F(4)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n + 1)-F(n + 2)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{60}-\left(\frac{1}{25 n + 60}\right)\]

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n}{12 \left(5 n + 12\right)}\]

questions.title: A finite window with a nonzero limit
questions.prompt_html:
All summands below are taken only at indices where their denominators are nonzero.

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. For \(n\ge3\), use partial fractions and the method of differences to find \(\sum_{r=3}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{r^{2} - 4}\right)\).

    [5]

  2. Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.

    [1]

  3. Evaluate

    \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{r=n + 1}^{3 n}\left(\frac{n}{r^{2} - 4}\right).\]
    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{r^{2} - 4}=\frac{1}{4 r - 8}-\left(\frac{1}{4 r + 8}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{4 r - 8}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(3)-F(7)]\\&\quad+[F(4)-F(8)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 4)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 4 and last 4 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{16}-\left(\frac{1}{4 n - 4}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 4}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 8}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{\left(n - 2\right) \left(25 n^{3} + 52 n^{2} + 7 n - 12\right)}{48 n \left(n - 1\right) \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}\]

(b)

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{\left(n - 2\right) \left(25 n^{3} + 52 n^{2} + 7 n - 12\right)}{48 n \left(n - 1\right) \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{25}{48}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.

(c)

First keep the window finite:

\[T_n=n\big(S_{3n}-S_n\big)\]
\[T_n=\frac n4\left[\frac1{n-1}+\frac1n+\frac1{n+1}+\frac1{n+2}-\frac1{3n-1}-\frac1{3n}-\frac1{3n+1}-\frac1{3n+2}\right].\]

The four positive scaled fractions tend to 1; the four subtracted scaled fractions tend to \(\frac{1}{3}\). Hence

\[\lim T_n=\frac14\left(4-\frac43\right)=\frac23.\]

questions.title: Challenge: two geometric differences
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(t\in\mathbb R\) and define

\[a_r=(2t)^r+(5t)^r,\qquad u_r=a_r-a_{r+1}.\]

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Find \(S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r\) in terms of \(t\) and \(n\).

    [3]

  2. Determine every real value of \(t\) for which the infinite series converges, and give its sum in each case.

    [5]

  3. Find all values of \(t\) for which the sum to infinity equals \(2/5\).

    [3]

  4. Set \(t=1/10\). Find the least integer \(n\) for which \(S_\infty-S_n\lt 10^{-4}\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[S_n=7 t - \left(2 t\right)^{n + 1} - \left(5 t\right)^{n + 1}\]

(b)

\[-\frac15\lt t\le\frac15.\]

For \(-\frac15\lt t\lt \frac15\), the sum is \(7t\). At \(t=1/5\), it is \(2/5\).

(c)

\[t=\frac{2}{35}\quad\text{or}\quad t=\frac15.\]

(d)

\(n=13\)
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Separate the two geometric differences. In each, only the first term and final subtracted term survive:

\[S_n=2t-(2t)^{n+1}+5t-(5t)^{n+1}.\]
\[S_n=7 t - \left(2 t\right)^{n + 1} - \left(5 t\right)^{n + 1}\]

(b)

When \(|5t|\lt 1\), both final powers tend to zero, so the sum is \(7t\). At \(t=1/5\), the term \((5t)^{n+1}\) is identically 1 while \((2t)^{n+1}\to0\), giving \(7/5-1=2/5\).

At \(t=-1/5\), the surviving \((-1)^{n+1}\) term oscillates, so no limit exists. If \(|t|\gt 1/5\), factor the two powers as

\[(5t)^{n+1}\left[1+(2/5)^{n+1}\right].\]

Its magnitude grows without bound; the smaller power cannot cancel the dominant one. These cases exhaust the real line.

(c)

In the open interval solve \(7t=2/5\), giving \(t=2/35\). This lies in the required interval. The separately evaluated endpoint \(t=1/5\) also gives the prescribed sum.

(d)

The exact positive remainder is

\[R_n=(1/5)^{n+1}+(1/2)^{n+1}.\]

It is strictly decreasing. At \(n=12\), \(R_{12}\gt 2^{-13}\gt 10^{-4}\). At \(n=13\), \(R_{13}=5^{-14}+2^{-14}\lt 10^{-4}\). Therefore 13 is the least value.

questions.title: A lower limit chosen to avoid poles
questions.prompt_html:
Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Express \(\frac{2}{r \left(r - 2\right) \left(r - 1\right)}\) in partial fractions.

    [3]

  2. For \(n\ge3\), find \(\sum_{r=3}^{n}\left(\frac{2}{r \left(r - 2\right) \left(r - 1\right)}\right)\).

    [2]

  3. Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

After clearing denominators, put \(r=2,1,0\) in turn. The corresponding coefficients are \(1,-2,1\).

\[\frac{2}{r \left(r - 2\right) \left(r - 1\right)}=- \frac{2}{r - 1} + \frac{1}{r - 2} + \frac{1}{r}\]

(b)

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{2}{r \left(r - 2\right) \left(r - 1\right)}=\frac{1}{\left(r - 2\right) \left(r - 1\right)}-\left(\frac{1}{r \left(r - 1\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{\left(r - 2\right) \left(r - 1\right)}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(3)-F(4)]\\&\quad+[F(4)-F(5)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{2}-\left(\frac{1}{n \left(n - 1\right)}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{\left(n - 2\right) \left(n + 1\right)}{2 n \left(n - 1\right)}\]

(c)

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{\left(n - 2\right) \left(n + 1\right)}{2 n \left(n - 1\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{1}{2}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.

  2. Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

questions.title: Induction followed by a strict remainder bound
questions.prompt_html:
Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Prove by mathematical induction that

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{2 r + 5}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)=\frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{\left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\]

    for every positive integer \(n\).

    [6]

  2. Hence prove that

    \[\sum_{r=n + 1}^{2 n}\left(\frac{2 r + 5}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)\lt \frac3{4n^2}.\]
    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The identity holds for all positive integers \(n\).

(b)

\[\sum_{r=n + 1}^{2 n}\left(\frac{2 r + 5}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)=\frac{3 n}{4 \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\lt \frac3{4n^2}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Base case. For \(n=1\), the left side is \(\frac{7}{120}\); the right side is \(1/8-1/15=7/120\).

Inductive hypothesis. Assume the formula is true at \(n=k\), for an arbitrary positive integer \(k\).

\[S_{k+1}=\frac18-\frac1{(k+2)(k+4)}+\frac{2k+7}{(k+2)(k+3)(k+4)(k+5)}.\]

The last two terms combine to

\[\frac{-(k+3)(k+5)+(2k+7)}{(k+2)(k+3)(k+4)(k+5)}=\frac{-(k+2)(k+4)}{(k+2)(k+3)(k+4)(k+5)}=-\frac1{(k+3)(k+5)}.\]

Thus \(S_{k+1}=1/8-1/[(k+3)(k+5)]\), exactly the required formula at \(k+1\). The base case and implication prove the result for every positive integer.

(b)

Subtract the two partial sums:

\[S_{2n}-S_n=\frac1{(n+2)(n+4)}-\frac1{(2n+2)(2n+4)}=\frac{3n}{4(n+1)(n+2)(n+4)}.\]

Since \((n+1)(n+2)(n+4)\gt n^3\gt 0\), the result is strictly less than \(3/(4n^2)\).
questions.hint_html:
1. After adding u_(k+1), combine only the two remainder fractions.

  2. Use the exact finite window, then compare three positive factors with n.

For \(0\lt x\lt 1\), the sum is \(-2^{\ln x}\). At \(x=1\) it is 0.

(c)

\[\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n=\frac{N \left(N + 1\right) \left(N^{2} + 9 N + 28\right)}{4}\]

(a)

All intermediate powers cancel:

\[[x^{f(2)}-x^{f(1)}]+[x^{f(3)}-x^{f(2)}]+\cdots+[x^{f(n+1)}-x^{f(n)}].\]

(b)

Use \(x^{\ln(r+1)}=(r+1)^{\ln x}\) to get

\[S_n=(n+2)^{\ln x}-2^{\ln x}.\]

For \(0\lt x\lt 1\), the exponent \(\ln x\) is negative, so the first term tends to zero. At \(x=1\) it is constantly 1 and the difference is zero. For \(x\gt 1\) it grows without bound.

(c)

Because \(x\gt 0\) and \(x\ne1\),

\[x^{3\log_x(r+1)}=(r+1)^3,\qquad S_n=(n+2)^3-8=n^3+6n^2+12n.\]
\[\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n=\frac{N^2(N+1)^2}{4}+N(N+1)(2N+1)+6N(N+1).\]
\[\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n=\frac{N \left(N + 1\right) \left(N^{2} + 9 N + 28\right)}{4}\]
questions.hint_html:
1. Keep the order of the difference as written.

  2. The sign of ln x controls the power of n+2.

  3. First simplify S_n, then apply the standard formulae to the second sum.

questions.title: Exponential differences and logarithmic sums
questions.prompt_html:
For a nonzero real constant \(x\), define

\[u_r=e^{2rx}(e^{2x}-1)^2.\]

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(u_r\right)\) in terms of \(n\) and \(x\).

    [4]

  2. For nonzero real \(x\), determine when the infinite series converges and find its sum.

    [2]

  3. Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\ln u_r\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(q=e^{2x}\), so \(q\gt 0\) and \(q\ne1\). Then

\[u_r=q^r(q-1)^2=(q-1)(q^{r+1}-q^r).\]

The geometric differences cancel:

\[S_n=(q-1)(q^{n+1}-q)=q(q-1)(q^n-1).\]

Replace \(q\) by \(e^{2x}\).

(b)

If \(x\lt 0\), then \(0\lt q\lt 1\) and \(q^n\to0\), so \(S=q(1-q)\). If \(x\gt 0\), then \(q\gt 1\) and the positive partial sums diverge to infinity.

(c)

For every allowed \(x\), \(u_r\gt 0\). The square must be handled with an absolute value:

\[\ln u_r=2rx+2\ln|e^{2x}-1|.\]

Summing gives \(2x\cdot n(n+1)/2\) plus \(n\) copies of the logarithmic constant.
questions.hint_html:
1. Factor out q−1 after setting q=e^(2x).

  2. The variable x is an exponent, so x<0 corresponds to a ratio below 1.

  3. Use ln(z²)=2 ln|z|; z may be negative.

questions.title: A tangent telescope that does not converge
questions.prompt_html:
For every integer \(r\ge0\), put \(A_r=r\pi/3+\pi/12\) and

\[u_r=\frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{\cos A_r\cos(A_r+\pi/3)}.\]

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Show that \(u_r=\tan(A_r+\pi/3)-\tan A_r\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(S_n=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}u_r\).

    [2]

  3. Prove that the infinite series does not converge.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\tan B-\tan A=\frac{\sin B\cos A-\cos B\sin A}{\cos A\cos B}=\frac{\sin(B-A)}{\cos A\cos B}.\]

Use \(B=A_r+\pi/3\). The denominators are nonzero: their angles have numerators \(4r+1\) or \(4r+5\) in units of \(\pi/12\), never \(6+12m\).

(b)

Since \(A_{r+1}=A_r+\pi/3\), the sum is \(\tan A_n-\tan A_0\).

(c)

\[S_{3m}=0,\qquad S_{3m+1}=\tan\frac{5\pi}{12}-\tan\frac\pi{12}=2\sqrt3.\]

The two infinite subsequences have different constant values, so the partial sums cannot have a common limit.

questions.title: A logarithmic total and a sharp accuracy cutoff
questions.prompt_html:
\[S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\ln\frac{(r+1)(r+3)}{(r+2)^2}.\]

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Find \(S_n\) and its limit \(S\).

    [4]

  2. Find the least \(n\) such that \(S_n-S\lt 0.002\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Split each logarithm as

\[\ln\frac{(r+1)(r+3)}{(r+2)^2}=\ln\frac{r+1}{r+2}-\ln\frac{r+2}{r+3}.\]

The difference telescopes to

\[S_n=\ln\frac23-\ln\frac{n+2}{n+3}=\ln\frac{2(n+3)}{3(n+2)}.\]

All logarithm arguments are positive. Taking the limit yields \(\ln(2/3)\).

(b)

\[S_n-S=\ln\left(1+\frac1{n+2}\right).\]

Because the exponential function is increasing,

\[\ln\left(1+\frac1{n+2}\right)\lt 0.002\iff n\gt \frac1{e^{0.002}-1}-2\approx497.5002.\]

Thus \(n=498\). At \(n=497\) the error is \(\ln(500/499)\gt 0.002\); at \(n=498\) it is \(\ln(501/500)\lt 0.002\).
questions.hint_html:
1. Use a difference of logarithms of consecutive ratios.

  2. Exponentiate the inequality rather than replacing ln(1+z) by z.

questions.title: A secant telescope with periodic partial sums
questions.prompt_html:
For integers \(r\ge0\), let

\[u_r=\frac{\sin(r\pi/3+\pi/4)}{\cos(r\pi/3+\pi/12)\cos(r\pi/3+5\pi/12)}.\]

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Use a sum-to-product identity to show that

    \[u_r=\sec\left(\frac{r\pi}{3}+\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)-\sec\left(\frac{r\pi}{3}+\frac\pi{12}\right).\]

  2. Find \(\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}u_r\).

(a)

\[\cos A-\cos B=2\sin\frac{A+B}{2}\sin\frac{B-A}{2}=\sin\left(\frac{r\pi}{3}+\frac\pi4\right).\]

(b)

The two arguments in each difference are successive members of the same angle sequence. All intermediate secants cancel.

(c)

\[S_{6m}=0,\qquad S_{6m+3}=-2\sec\frac\pi{12}.\]

questions.title: Fourth powers of consecutive odd integers
questions.prompt_html:
Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Use standard summation formulae to simplify

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(64 r^{3} + 16 r\right)\]

    in terms of \(n\).

    [3]

  2. Use the method of differences to find

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{64 r^{3} + 16 r}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4} \left(2 r + 1\right)^{4}}\right)\]

    in terms of \(n\).

    [4]

  3. Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(64 r^{3} + 16 r\right)=8 n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)\]

(b)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{64 r^{3} + 16 r}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4} \left(2 r + 1\right)^{4}}\right)=\frac{8 n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{4}}\]

(c)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{64 r^{3} + 16 r}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4} \left(2 r + 1\right)^{4}}\right)=1\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[64 r^{3} + 16 r=64 r^{3} + 16 r\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(64 r^{3} + 16 r\right)=64\left(\frac{n^{2} \left(n + 1\right)^{2}}{4}\right)+16\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(64 r^{3} + 16 r\right)=8 n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)\]

(b)

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{64 r^{3} + 16 r}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4} \left(2 r + 1\right)^{4}}=\frac{1}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4}}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(2 r + 1\right)^{4}}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{\left(2 r - 1\right)^{4}}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=1-\left(\frac{1}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{4}}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{8 n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{4}}\]

(c)

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{8 n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)}{\left(2 n + 1\right)^{4}}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=1\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
questions.hint_html:
1. Expand before applying the standard summation formulae.

  2. Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

  3. Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.

questions.title: A linear numerator over three consecutive factors
questions.prompt_html:
Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Use standard summation formulae to simplify

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)\]

    in terms of \(n\).

    [3]

  2. Express \(\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\) in partial fractions. Hence find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)\).

    [4]

  3. Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 7\right) \left(n^{2} + 7 n + 22\right)}{4}\]

(b)

\[\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}=- \frac{2}{r + 4} + \frac{1}{r + 3} + \frac{1}{r + 2}\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)=\frac{n \left(5 n + 17\right)}{6 \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\]

(c)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}\right)=\frac{5}{6}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Expand the summand and separate its powers of \(r\).

\[\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)=r^{3} + 9 r^{2} + 26 r + 24\]

Use the standard formulae; the constant is counted once for each of the \(n\) terms.

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)=1\left(\frac{n^{2} \left(n + 1\right)^{2}}{4}\right)+9\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 1\right)}{6}\right)+26\left(\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}\right)+24\left(n\right)\]
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)\right)=\frac{n \left(n + 7\right) \left(n^{2} + 7 n + 22\right)}{4}\]

(b)

The simple partial fractions are

\[\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}=- \frac{2}{r + 4} + \frac{1}{r + 3} + \frac{1}{r + 2}\]

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{3 r + 8}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 3\right) \left(r + 4\right)}=\frac{2}{r + 3} + \frac{1}{r + 2}-\left(\frac{2}{r + 4} + \frac{1}{r + 3}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{2}{r + 3} + \frac{1}{r + 2}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{5}{6}-\left(\frac{2}{n + 4} + \frac{1}{n + 3}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(5 n + 17\right)}{6 \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\]

(c)

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(5 n + 17\right)}{6 \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{5}{6}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.

questions.title: A radical remainder with a least-index condition
questions.prompt_html:
Let

\[a_r=\frac{r+3}{\sqrt{r^2+2r+2}}-\frac{r+4}{\sqrt{r^2+4r+5}},\qquad S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}a_r.\]

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  2. Find the least \(n\) for which

    \[S_n\gt \frac4{\sqrt5}-\frac{21}{20}.\]

questions.solution_html:
(a)

The cancellation gives

\[S_n=\frac4{\sqrt5}-\frac{n+4}{\sqrt{n^2+4n+5}}.\]
\[S_{25}=\frac4{\sqrt5}-\frac{29}{\sqrt{730}}\approx 0.715516.\]

The inequality reduces to

\[\frac{n+4}{\sqrt{n^2+4n+5}}\lt \frac{21}{20}.\]

Put \(m=n+2\ge3\). Both sides are positive, so squaring is equivalent:

\[400(m+2)^2\lt 441(m^2+1)\iff41m^2-1600m-1159\gt 0.\]

The function \((m+2)/\sqrt{m^2+1}\) decreases for \(m\ge3\), since its derivative is \((1-2m)/(m^2+1)^{3/2}\lt 0\). At \(m=39\) the quadratic is −1198; at \(m=40\) it is 441. Thus the least allowed \(m\) is 40, giving \(n=38\).

questions.title: Three arctangent boundary terms
questions.prompt_html:
Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. For \(z\gt 0\), prove that

    \[\arctan(z+3)-\arctan z=\arctan\frac3{z^2+3z+1}.\]
    [3]

  2. Hence find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\arctan\frac3{r^2+3r+1}\).

    [3]

  3. Deduce the sum to infinity, simplifying your answer.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(A=\arctan(z+3)\) and \(B=\arctan z\). The tangent difference formula gives

\[\tan(A-B)=\frac{(z+3)-z}{1+z(z+3)}=\frac3{z^2+3z+1}.\]

Since \(0\lt B\lt A\lt \pi/2\), the difference lies in \((0,\pi/2)\). Therefore the principal arctangent gives exactly \(A-B\), with no extra multiple of \(\pi\).

(b)

Replace each term by \(\arctan(r+3)-\arctan r\). Three terms remain at each end after cancellation, giving the stated answer.

(c)

Each upper arctangent tends to \(\pi/2\). Also \(\arctan1+\arctan2+\arctan3=\pi\): the first two angles have tangent −3 and their sum is in \((\pi/2,\pi)\), so their sum is \(\pi-\arctan3\). Thus the total is \(3\pi/2-\pi=\pi/2\).

1. Establish the range of the angle difference, not only equality of tangents.

  2. This is a three-step difference, so retain three boundary angles.

  3. Use the branch-correct identity arctan1+arctan2+arctan3=π.

questions.title: A logarithmic sum with a separate endpoint
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(x\ge-1\) be real and define

\[u_r=\ln\frac{2+x^{r+1}}{2+x^r}.\]

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Find \(S_N=\sum_{r=1}^{N}u_r\).

    [2]

  2. Determine every allowed real \(x\) for which the infinite series converges, and give its sum in each case.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[S_N=\ln\frac{2+x^{N+1}}{2+x}.\]

(b)

\[-1\lt x\le1.\]

For \(-1\lt x\lt 1\), the sum is \(\ln[2/(2+x)]\). At \(x=1\) the sum is 0.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

All logarithm arguments are positive on the stated domain. Split each term into two logarithms:

\[u_r=\ln(2+x^{r+1})-\ln(2+x^r).\]

Cancellation gives \(\ln(2+x^{N+1})-\ln(2+x)\).

(b)

If \(|x|\lt 1\), then \(x^{N+1}\to0\) and the sum is \(\ln[2/(2+x)]\). At \(x=1\) every summand is zero.

At \(x=-1\), partial sums alternate between 0 and \(\ln3\), so there is no limit. For \(x\gt 1\) the numerator inside the logarithm grows without bound, giving divergence to infinity.
questions.hint_html:
1. Use differences of logarithms of successive terms.

  2. Do not substitute x=1 into the formula derived from |x|<1.

Exclude x=−1 and x>1 with valid reasons.

questions.title: Four starting terms in a reciprocal sum
questions.prompt_html:
Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Use the method of differences to find

    \[\sum_{r=0}^{n - 1}\left(\frac{1}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 6\right)}\right)\]

    in terms of \(n\).

    [4]

  2. Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{1}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(r + 6\right)}=\frac{1}{4 r + 8}-\left(\frac{1}{4 r + 24}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{4 r + 8}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(0)-F(4)]\\&\quad+[F(1)-F(5)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n - 1)-F(n + 3)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 4 and last 4 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{20}-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 8}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 12}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 16}\right)-\left(\frac{1}{4 n + 20}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(77 n^{3} + 838 n^{2} + 2947 n + 3338\right)}{240 \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right) \left(n + 5\right)}\]

(b)

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(77 n^{3} + 838 n^{2} + 2947 n + 3338\right)}{240 \left(n + 2\right) \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 4\right) \left(n + 5\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{77}{240}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.

1. Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

  2. Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.

questions.title: A difference between two quadratic denominators
questions.prompt_html:
\[F(r)=\frac{1}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(3 r + 2\right)},\qquad u_r=\frac{6 r + 8}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 5\right)}.\]

Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Verify that \(u_r=F(r)-F(r+1)\).

    [2]

  2. Use the method of differences to find

    \[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{6 r + 8}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 5\right)}\right)\]

    in terms of \(n\).

    [3]

  3. Determine whether the corresponding infinite series converges and, if it does, find its sum.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The identity holds.

(b)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{6 r + 8}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 5\right)}\right)=\frac{n \left(3 n + 11\right)}{10 \left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 5\right)}\]

(c)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{6 r + 8}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 5\right)}\right)=\frac{1}{10}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The common numerator is

\[(r+2)(3r+5)-(r+1)(3r+2)=6r+8=2(3r+4).\]

(b)

Use the following difference, obtained by combining the terms over a common denominator:

\[\frac{6 r + 8}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 5\right)}=\frac{1}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(3 r + 2\right)}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(r + 2\right) \left(3 r + 5\right)}\right)\]

Writing \(F(r)=\frac{1}{\left(r + 1\right) \left(3 r + 2\right)}\) and denoting the requested finite sum by \(S_n\), the cancellation is

\[\begin{aligned}S_n&=[F(1)-F(2)]\\&\quad+[F(2)-F(3)]+\cdots\\&\quad+[F(n)-F(n + 1)].\end{aligned}\]

Only the first 1 and last 1 boundary terms remain (the formula also covers overlapping boundaries).

\[S_n=\frac{1}{10}-\left(\frac{1}{\left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 5\right)}\right)\]
\[S_n=\frac{n \left(3 n + 11\right)}{10 \left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 5\right)}\]

(c)

The partial sums satisfy

\[S_n=\frac{n \left(3 n + 11\right)}{10 \left(n + 2\right) \left(3 n + 5\right)}\]

Taking the limit as \(n\to\infty\) gives a finite number:

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n=\frac{1}{10}\]

Therefore the series converges to this value.
questions.hint_html:
1. Subtract the two products after taking a common denominator.

  2. Find a difference F(r)−F(r+h), then write the boundary terms before simplifying.

  3. Use the finite partial sum, not a sum of separate divergent series.

questions.title: A cosine sum with no infinite limit
questions.prompt_html:
Unless stated otherwise, \(n\) and \(N\) are positive integers. Give exact answers and show your reasoning.

  1. Use the identity

    \[\sin[(2r+1)\theta]-\sin[(2r-1)\theta]=2\sin\theta\cos(2r\theta)\]

    to find \(\sum_{r=1}^{N}\cos(2r\theta)\), where \(\theta\) is not an integer multiple of \(\pi\).

    [3]

  2. Set \(\theta=\pi/4\). Show that the infinite cosine series does not converge.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Sum the identity over \(r=1,\ldots,N\). Every internal sine cancels, giving

\[2\sin\theta\sum_{r=1}^{N}\cos(2r\theta)=\sin[(2N+1)\theta]-\sin\theta.\]

Division by \(2\sin\theta\) is valid because \(\theta\notin\pi\mathbb Z\).

(b)

Its terms repeat \(0,-1,0,1\). Consequently,

\[S_{4m}=0,\qquad S_{4m+2}=-1.\]

These two subsequences have different limits, so the partial sums do not converge.
questions.hint_html:
1. The restriction on θ is needed before dividing by sinθ.

  2. Use two subsequences of partial sums, rather than relying on the word “oscillates”.
